analysis.one_liner: Bars ticket sellers from locking venues into exclusive contracts lasting more than about four years.
analysis.headline: The bill to limit long-term exclusive ticketing contracts was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop ticket companies from signing exclusive contracts that lock a venue's entire ticket sale business to one provider for an excessive length of time, which the Federal Trade Commission would define as anything longer than four years at minimum. It aims to break up the long-term exclusivity deals that keep rival ticket sellers out of major arenas, a system that drew national attention after the 2022 Taylor Swift ticket sale meltdown. Violating companies would face civil penalties enforced by the FTC.
analysis.who_benefits: Concertgoers and other ticket buyers gain if more companies can compete to sell tickets for the same arenas and stadiums, which could mean more choices, better service, and pressure on service fees. Performers, promoters, and venues that want to switch providers or run their own box office would gain bargaining power. Rival ticketing companies would gain access to venues currently locked up by long exclusive deals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ticket buyers and rival ticket sellers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a primary ticketing provider from holding an exclusive contract to sell all or nearly all tickets for a venue if the contract runs longer than an 'excessive duration,' which the FTC must define at a minimum of more than four years [S2][S3].

Gives the FTC enforcement powers under the Federal Trade Commission Act and authorizes civil penalties against violating ticketing companies, sized to deter violations but capped at the volume of commerce affected [S3].
Covers all venues seating at least 5,000 people for concerts, theater, sports, and comedy, which is where the live-events ticketing market is most concentrated [S3].
Leaves existing antitrust laws fully intact, so this adds a targeted tool rather than replacing broader competition enforcement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The dominant ticketing company holding long exclusive venue contracts would lose those locked-in deals once they exceed the permitted length. Some venues would give up large upfront payments and guaranteed advances that long exclusivity deals bring in exchange for more competition. The FTC would bear the cost of writing rules and enforcing them, paid for by taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dominant ticketing companies and some venues

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban exclusive contracts outright, only overly long ones, so a dominant company could still hold venues with a series of shorter deals if it remains the most attractive partner [S3].

Venues often receive substantial upfront payments, capital investments, or guaranteed advances in exchange for long exclusivity; capping contract length could mean less guaranteed revenue for arenas, which some venues would pass on through rent or ticket costs.

The FTC must define 'excessive duration' through rulemaking, and a duration set too short could disrupt venue financing, while the cap on civil penalties at the volume of commerce affected could limit deterrence for a company with enormous revenue [S3].

More competition among ticket sellers does not guarantee lower prices or fees for fans, since ticket prices are largely set by performers and promoters and fees are disclosed late in the purchase process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real but modest: weakening long exclusivity locks could open the largest venues to competing ticket sellers and give fans a fallback when one system fails, as happened in the widely publicized Taylor Swift on-sale. The costs fall mainly on the dominant ticketing company and on venues that trade exclusivity for upfront money. The bill's main design weakness is that it targets duration rather than exclusivity itself, so its impact depends heavily on how the FTC writes the rules and how hard it enforces them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day and never moved; no hearing, no vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill with Senator Richard Blumenthal as its only cosponsor on April 26, 2023 [S1][S3][S4].
That same day the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, where no further action was ever taken [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the committee holding a hearing or the Senate voting on the bill, so it died [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The dominant ticketing company is better off: its long exclusive venue contracts faced no new legal limit, and no competitor gained access to locked-up arenas. Fans and rival sellers are no better off than before.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.role: Sponsor; chair of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Competition Policy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap exclusive venue ticketing contract durations and gave it a high-profile rollout after the 2022 Ticketmaster scrutiny

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup was ever held in the 21 months before the Congress ended

against.name: Live Nation / Ticketmaster
against.role: Dominant primary ticketing provider whose long exclusive venue contracts the bill targets
against.what_they_did: Publicly defended its long-term venue contracts as beneficial to venues and opposed efforts to restrict them

sides.party_line_note: Both named supporters are Democrats and no Republican signed on, but no vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of the full Senate is unknown.

industries.note: The bill directly targets the long exclusive venue contracts that lock arenas and stadiums to one ticket seller for years at a time, threatening the dominant company's core moat. It adds FTC enforcement and civil penalties on top of existing antitrust law [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Large event venues (arenas and stadiums over 5,000 seats)
industries.note: Venues trade long exclusivity for upfront payments, advances, and capital investment from ticketing companies; the bill would cap that trade-off while potentially bringing them competing bids and better service. Fans benefit if venues gain real choice [S3].

industries.industry: Rival ticketing and live-event technology companies
industries.note: Competitors would get the chance to bid for contracts at major venues currently locked up for four-plus-year terms, expanding the market for alternatives [S2][S3].
